proposal.title: AP: More Than Two Dozen Military Leaders Were Fired or Pushed to Retire
proposal.description_short: AP reported more than two dozen military leaders were fired or pushed to retire under Trump or Hegseth.
proposal.description_medium: An Associated Press report published by ABC News said President Donald Trump or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office. AP described a mix of firings and pressured retirements and named the Army’s top uniformed officer among those affected. The report does not establish one reason for every departure.
proposal.description_long: An Associated Press report published by ABC News on September 30, 2026, said President Donald Trump or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office. The report describes a mixed category of departures: some were firings, while others were leaders pushed to retire. It names the Army’s top uniformed officer among those affected. The count should remain attributed to AP and should not be rewritten as a count of people formally fired. The cited article is reporting, not an official personnel tally reproduced here. It does not establish that every departure had the same cause, that political loyalty determined who left, or that the changes produced a measured effect on readiness. The Hill article previously considered discusses planned senior-rank cuts, but prior source review found it does not independently substantiate this past-departure count. This proposal therefore cites the AP-syndicated ABC News report for the count and its mixed categories.

source_to_fact_mappings.supports: AP-syndicated report says Trump or Hegseth fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders, including the Army’s top uniformed officer among affected leaders.
source_to_fact_mappings.does_not_support: A count of formal firings alone; one common motive, political targeting, or a measured readiness effect.
source_to_fact_mappings.access_basis: Prior worker-02 source review recorded Exa cached exact-URL text/highlights for the AP-syndicated ABC News report; coordinator row also maps this URL to the count.

reasons: Narrowed the count to attributed AP reporting and kept firings distinct from pressured retirements.
Removed The Hill from the citation list because prior QA found it supplies planned-cut context but does not independently substantiate the past-departure count.
The original Slate and Wikipedia links do not support this count and are excluded.

proposal.title: Trump Removes State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
proposal.description_short: Trump removed Steve Linick as State Department inspector general in May 2020 amid oversight inquiries involving Pompeo.
proposal.description_medium: Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020. Congressional Democrats said his office had inquiries involving Secretary Mike Pompeo and raised concern about possible retaliation. NBC reported that the inquiries concerned Pompeo’s alleged personal errands and the Saudi arms-sale emergency. Pompeo said he recommended the removal; the White House cited lack of confidence.
proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020. A Senate Foreign Relations Committee release records lawmakers’ concern that the firing could be retaliation connected to oversight of Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, and says they sought records about the removal and open matters. NBC News reported that Linick’s office was examining alleged Pompeo personal errands and the emergency Saudi arms-sale process. NBC also reported that Pompeo said he recommended Linick’s removal and denied knowing about one inquiry, while Trump’s notification cited a lack of confidence. These are competing attributed accounts, not a finding that retaliation occurred. The sources establish the removal and the oversight context; they do not establish motive from timing alone. The unrelated USA Today wildfire URL in the earlier staged record is excluded. This account keeps only the Senate release and NBC report as support, distinguishes the lawmakers’ allegation from established fact, and does not infer a corrupt purpose.

source_to_fact_mappings.supports: May 2020 removal and Senate Democrats’ concern/request for records about possible retaliation and ongoing matters.
source_to_fact_mappings.does_not_support: An independent finding that retaliation occurred.
source_to_fact_mappings.access_basis: Prior worker-02 QA recorded a Firecrawl direct scrape of this exact URL.

source_to_fact_mappings.supports: Linick office inquiries into alleged Pompeo personal errands and the Saudi arms-sale emergency; Pompeo recommendation/denial and Trump notification citing lack of confidence.

proposal.title: Trump Pardoned William E. Henry on January 19, 2021
proposal.description_short: DOJ lists William E. “Ed” Henry among Trump’s pardons granted January 19, 2021, for a federal theft-of-government-property conviction.
proposal.description_medium: The Justice Department lists William E. “Ed” Henry among the pardons President Donald Trump granted on January 19, 2021. DOJ identifies a Middle District of Alabama conviction for theft of government property under 18 U.S.C. § 641 and lists two years’ probation, a $4,000 fine and a $100 special assessment. The listing does not specify clemency terms or explain Trump’s rationale.
proposal.description_long: The U.S. Department of Justice’s public listing of pardons granted by President Donald Trump identifies William E. “Ed” Henry among people pardoned on January 19, 2021. DOJ lists a federal conviction in the Middle District of Alabama for theft of government property under 18 U.S.C. § 641. It records a sentence of two years’ probation, a $4,000 fine and a $100 special assessment. These details are stated as the DOJ listing records them; the page is not a narrative of the underlying conduct. It supports saying Henry received a pardon on that date, but does not reproduce a grant instrument or specify whether the pardon was full or unconditional. The listing also gives no reason Trump selected Henry and does not connect clemency to money or political assistance. The revised account stays with the official clemency entry and listed conviction and sentence. It leaves the offense’s underlying facts and the President’s rationale unstated, because this citation does not document either.

source_to_fact_mappings.supports: DOJ lists William “Ed” Henry among January 19, 2021 pardons and identifies the Middle District of Alabama theft-of-government-property conviction and listed sentence.
source_to_fact_mappings.does_not_support: The terms “full” or “unconditional”; underlying conduct beyond the listed offense; Trump’s rationale; an improper exchange.
source_to_fact_mappings.access_basis: Prior worker-02 QA records the official DOJ clemency listing as reviewed and directly scraped; the proposed instrument URL had returned 504 in that review and is not relied on.

reasons: Removed “full” and “unconditional”; the exact DOJ list establishes a pardon but does not specify those terms.
Retained only date, identity, listed conviction and sentence; no motive or corrupt exchange is inferred.
The inaccessible grant-instrument response is not treated as verified text or as support.

proposal.title: Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner Spent a Day on David Geffen’s Yacht in Croatia
proposal.description_short: TIME reported Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner spent a day in Croatia aboard David Geffen’s yacht with Wendi Deng in August 2016.
proposal.description_medium: TIME’s August 17, 2016 report says Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner spent a day in Croatia aboard David Geffen’s yacht and went sightseeing with Wendi Deng. This contemporaneous account supports the outing and named company. It does not support the original headline’s claim that the pair met a Russian oligarch.
proposal.description_long: TIME’s August 17, 2016 story documents a day in Croatia for Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner aboard David Geffen’s yacht, with Wendi Deng joining them for sightseeing. Those specifics—the couple, the setting, the yacht and the named companion—are what the cited report supports. The story does not report a meeting with a Russian oligarch, identify such a person, or say one was present. The original TrumpFile headline joins that separate encounter allegation to the documented vacation, but the verified TIME article cannot substantiate the added claim. The revised title and descriptions retain the documented outing and omit the alleged meeting. They also avoid inferring a political purpose or improper contact from the trip or from Deng’s presence. The packet does not include an underlying interview record that could verify the alleged meeting. Without such support, this longer description is confined to the reported outing and the distinction between it and the unsupported encounter claim.

source_to_fact_mappings.supports: TIME’s August 17, 2016 report that Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner spent a day on David Geffen’s yacht in Croatia with Wendi Deng, including sightseeing.
source_to_fact_mappings.does_not_support: A Russian-oligarch meeting, identity/presence of an alleged oligarch, political purpose, or improper contact.
source_to_fact_mappings.access_basis: Prior worker-02 QA recorded a direct Firecrawl scrape; page returned HTTP 200 and article text identified the outing.

reasons: Kept the contemporaneously reported Croatia outing and removed the unsupported Russian-oligarch meeting claim.
